3.1.summary:
It isn't only that life gets shorter every day. If you live long, your mind may start failing before your body does. You'll go on eating, breathing and wanting things, but the ability to think clearly, judge well and do your duty can fade first.

So don't put off the work of becoming wise. The window for it may close sooner than death.

3.2.summary:
Even nature's by-products have their own beauty: the cracks in a loaf's crust, figs splitting when ripe, olives close to rotting, drooping ears of corn, a lion's frown, foam at a boar's mouth. On their own they're not pretty, but because they come from natural processes they add to the whole.

Someone who truly understands nature finds this everywhere: real animals as striking as their portraits, a mature grace in old age, and youth's beauty seen without lust.
3.2.today: Think of the wrinkles around a grandparent's eyes, a burnt edge on homemade bread, autumn leaves going brown, or a dog's grey muzzle. Seen properly, these aren't flaws but part of things running their natural course.

3.3.summary:
Everyone dies, however great. The physician Hippocrates cured many and then died of illness. Astrologers predicted others' deaths and met their own. Conquerors like Alexander and Julius Caesar, who killed thousands, died too. Philosophers died in undignified ways.

So treat life as a voyage: you've sailed, you've arrived, now step off. If there's another life, there are gods there too. If there's nothing, you're simply freed from pain, pleasure and serving a body far inferior to the mind within it.

3.4.summary:
Don't waste your remaining life wondering what others are doing, saying, thinking or plotting, unless it serves some common good. It keeps you from minding your own mind. A good test: only think things you'd happily admit if someone suddenly asked what was on your mind.

A person like that is steady, kind, fair, and accepts what life gives. They care for everyone, but don't chase praise from people who don't live well and aren't even satisfied with themselves.
3.4.today: Picture someone asking, mid-commute, 'What are you thinking about?' If the honest answer is a grudge against your sister-in-law or a theory about why a colleague got promoted, that's a sign. Picture the thought you'd be glad to say out loud instead.

3.5.summary:
Marcus gives himself a set of working rules: do your work willingly, for the common good, with thought, and without distraction. Don't dress up your thoughts in fancy words, don't talk too much, and don't take on too much. Be ready to leave life whenever the call comes, like a soldier at his post.

Be cheerful, and don't rely on others for support or peace of mind. Stand upright on your own; don't be propped up.
3.5.today: This might mean doing the dull report without sulking, keeping a meeting update to three sentences instead of ten, and turning down the fourth project you have no room for. Standing upright means not needing a colleague's reassurance before you feel okay.

3.6.summary:
If you can find anything better than justice, truth, self-control, courage and a mind at peace with acting rightly and accepting its lot, then go for it. But if nothing beats your own reason and conscience, don't let anything else compete with it, whether praise, power or pleasure. Once you start making room for them, they take over.

If someone says that the useful is the better, Marcus replies: useful to you as a thinking being, or only as an animal? Be honest about which.
3.6.today: The promotion that requires cutting ethical corners, or the popularity you'd gain by laughing along at a cruel joke, are the competitors Marcus means. They look like they fit alongside your values until, suddenly, they've pushed them aside.

3.7.summary:
Never treat something as good for you if it would make you break a promise, lose your self-respect, hate or suspect someone, curse, pretend, or want something that needs hiding behind closed doors. Someone who values their reason and integrity above everything doesn't make a drama of life, doesn't need either solitude or crowds, and neither chases death nor runs from it.

Whether they live long or short doesn't trouble them. All that matters is behaving like a thinking, social being to the end.
3.7.today: The deal that only works if you stay quiet about a flaw, the affair, or the browser history you'd be mortified to have seen all fail the test of 'needs walls and curtains'.

3.8.summary:
A mind that has been disciplined and cleaned out has nothing festering in it, no hidden wound, nothing slavish or fake. It's neither too attached to things nor cut off from them, and has nothing to hide.

And such a life is never incomplete when death comes. It isn't like an actor walking off before the play ends, because each part of it was already whole.

3.9.summary: Treasure your ability to form judgements. Whether you think in a way that suits a reasoning human being depends entirely on it. Used well, it keeps you from jumping to conclusions, makes you friendly towards others, and keeps you in step with the gods, or the way the universe works.

3.10.summary: Throw everything else away and keep these few principles. Remember that you only ever live in the present moment; the rest of life is either gone or uncertain. Life is short, the corner of the earth you live in is tiny, and even the longest fame after death is brief, passed on by people who will soon die themselves, who barely know themselves, let alone you.

3.11.summary:
Here's another tool: whenever something affects you, define it plainly. Strip it down to what it really is, what it's made of, what it will break down into, and how long it will last. Ask what part it plays in the universe and which quality it calls for in you: patience, courage, honesty, simplicity.

And sort what happens: some comes from the universe's order, some from chance, and some from other people. They're your kin, even if they don't know how to behave, so treat them kindly and fairly.
3.11.today: A rude email becomes some words on a screen from a stressed person, gone from memory in a week, calling for patience. A bigger salary becomes numbers in an account. Describing things plainly takes the heat out of them.

3.12.summary: If you get on with the task in front of you, guided by reason, seriously and calmly, without distraction, and keep your inner self clean as if you had to hand it back at any moment, you'll live well. Expect nothing, fear nothing, be content with doing what's right, and speak the truth boldly. Nobody can stop you from living like this.
3.12.today: Washing up, writing a report or helping a child with homework can all be done this way: fully, honestly and without worrying about what you'll get for it or what might go wrong tomorrow.

3.13.summary: A doctor keeps instruments ready for emergencies. You should keep your principles just as ready, so you can understand what's happening and act well, even in small things. Remember too that human affairs and the larger order of the universe are bound together: you can't handle one well while ignoring the other.

3.14.summary:
Stop drifting. You'll never get round to reading your own notes, the histories of the Greeks and Romans, or the extracts you were saving for retirement. Drop the comfortable hopes, head for the goal you've set yourself, and come to your own rescue while you still can.

Marcus is talking to himself, and the tone is urgent. Planning to improve later is a way of not improving.
3.14.today: The reading list you're saving for the holidays, the language you'll learn once the children are older, the course for 'when things calm down': Marcus would say start now, with whatever time you actually have.

3.15.summary: People don't realise how much is packed into ordinary words like stealing, sowing, buying, keeping quiet, or seeing what needs to be done. Understanding them properly takes more than the eyes; it takes the mind's own kind of vision, which grasps what an action really is and what it means.

3.16.summary:
We have a body that senses, a soul that desires and a mind that reasons. Animals share the first; beasts and tyrants like Phalaris and Nero share the second; even traitors and hypocrites have the third, using their wits to get what they want.

What belongs to the good person alone is being content with what happens, keeping their inner self calm and following it honestly and justly. Even if nobody believes they live simply and contentedly, they aren't angry, and they walk calmly towards the end, ready to go.
